key_facts: **Urticaria**: itchy, transient **weals** (each lasting < 24 h) from mast-cell mediator release; **angioedema** is deeper swelling lasting up to 72 h.
About **1 in 5** people have acute urticaria in their lifetime; chronic spontaneous urticaria affects **0.5–2%**.
Acute (< 6 weeks) is often triggered by infection, drugs or food; chronic (≥ 6 weeks) is usually spontaneous or inducible.
UK first line: a **non-sedating second-generation antihistamine**, increased up to 4 times the licensed dose (off-label) under guidance.
Angioedema **without weals** (ACE inhibitor, hereditary) is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to antihistamines; airway swelling is an emergency.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Urticaria** is a transient, itchy eruption of wheals. **Acute** lasts under 6 weeks; **chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU)** lasts 6 weeks or more, most days. **Inducible (physical)** urticaria is triggered by pressure, heat, cold, sweat or stroking (dermographism).
**Angioedema** is deeper subcutaneous/submucosal swelling. It may accompany histaminergic urticaria or occur alone (ACE-inhibitor bradykinin angioedema; rare hereditary angioedema).

sub: About 20% lifetime prevalence; all ages and both sexes.
In children usually triggered by **viral infection**; in adults often idiopathic.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria affects **0.5–2%**, about two thirds women, peak 20–40 years.
Chronic inducible (physical) urticarias such as dermographism are more common.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria lasts on average 2–5 years; about half clear within a year.

ul: Mast-cell degranulation (IgE, autoimmune, idiopathic, or direct — NSAIDs, opioids, contrast).
CSU is usually not an IgE food allergy — restrictive diets and patch tests do not help.
ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin angioedema that can start months to years after initiation.
Inducible triggers: dermographism, delayed pressure, cholinergic, cold, solar, aquagenic.
**Acute triggers**: viral or bacterial infection, **drugs** (NSAIDs, aspirin, antibiotics, opioids), IgE-mediated food allergy (milk, egg, peanut, shellfish), insect stings.
**Chronic spontaneous**: autoimmune (IgG autoantibodies to IgE or its receptor FcεRI, or IgE to self-antigens) in about half; associated with autoimmune thyroid disease.
**Inducible**: dermographism, cold, cholinergic (heat, sweat), pressure, solar, aquagenic, vibratory.
**Aggravators**: NSAIDs, alcohol, heat, stress, tight clothing.
**"Chronic hives must be an allergy"**: chronic spontaneous urticaria is rarely allergic; extensive allergy testing is not helpful.
**"All swelling responds to antihistamines"**: bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema) does not.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Weals come from **mast cells** in the dermis releasing histamine and other mediators; angioedema is the same process deeper down (or bradykinin-driven).

mech.t: Triggers (IgE cross-linking by allergen, autoantibodies to FcεRI, complement, drugs, physical stimuli) activate dermal **mast cells** and basophils.
Mast cells degranulate, releasing **histamine**, prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor and cytokines.
mech.caption: A dermal mast cell releases histamine-containing granules; the nearby vessel leaks fluid, raising a weal.

mech.t: Histamine dilates and opens small vessels (**oedema and redness**: the weal and flare) and stimulates sensory nerves (**itch**).
mech.caption: Weal (superficial dermal oedema) vs angioedema (oedema of deep dermis and subcutis).

mech.t: The same leak in the **deep dermis, subcutis or mucosa** gives angioedema; **bradykinin** causes non-itchy angioedema without weals (ACE inhibitors, C1-inhibitor deficiency).
mech.caption: Angioedema of the lips and eyelids.

mech.t: Mediators are cleared within hours, so each weal fades within 24 hours without marks; lesions lasting longer or bruising suggest **urticarial vasculitis**.

histo: Dermal oedema with dilated vessels and a sparse perivascular infiltrate (neutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes); epidermis normal.
Biopsy only if weals last over 24 hours, burn or bruise (to exclude urticarial vasculitis).

ul: Wheals: itchy, pink or skin-coloured, migrate, **individually fade within 24 hours**, leave normal skin.
In skin of colour, feel for oedema when erythema is subtle.
Angioedema: lips, eyelids, hands, genitals — may burn more than itch.
Vasculitis clue: lesions >24 h, burning/pain, purpura or residual bruise.

variants.name: Acute urticaria
variants.t: Raised blanching wheals with flare. *Site: Anywhere.*

variants.name: Dermographism
variants.t: Linear wheals where skin is stroked. *Site: Trunk.*

variants.name: Cold urticaria
variants.t: Wheals on cold-exposed skin; warn about cold water. *Site: Exposed skin.*

variants.name: Cholinergic
variants.t: Small 2–5 mm wheals with flare on heat or exercise. *Site: Trunk.*

variants.name: Urticarial vasculitis
variants.t: > 24 h, burning, leaves bruising. *Site: Trunk, limbs.*

sub: Weals may look skin-coloured or slightly darker rather than red; rely on raised, itchy, transient swellings.
Loratadine or cetirizine are usually preferred (check BNF).

ul: Clinical history ± phone photos. Acute urticaria: **no routine tests**.
CSU: keep tests minimal — FBC and CRP/ESR reasonable; thyroid tests only if indicated. **Patch testing has no role** in urticaria.

ddx.name: Contact eczema
ddx.f: Scaly, lasting days; patch testing relevant.

ul: Remove triggers; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin/opioids if they aggravate; prefer paracetamol.
Cool measures; avoid overheating and tight clothes.
First-line: **cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine** at licensed daily dose — take **every day** in CSU, not only as needed.
If uncontrolled after 2–4 weeks: increase up to **four times** the licensed dose (off-label; counsel sedation risk at higher doses).
Switch agent if one fails at high dose. Short sedating antihistamine at night only when sleep is wrecked — not routine with high-dose non-sedating drugs.
Severe acute flare: short oral prednisolone (e.g. up to 7 days per CKS) **plus** antihistamine — avoid repeated courses in CSU.
Montelukast sometimes added on specialist advice (NSAID-aggravated/pressure). H2 blockers are no longer routine.

ACE-inhibitor angioedema ± without wheals: **stop the ACEI**; do not rechallenge; antihistamines/steroids help poorly — emergency care if airway threatened; switch to ARB only with caution and specialist advice.
Uncontrolled CSU → dermatology/allergy for **omalizumab** (NICE TA) then other immunosuppressants.
Pregnancy/breastfeeding/renal/hepatic dosing: check BNF carefully (cetirizine often favoured in pregnancy counselling themes — verify current advice).

blocks.title: Anaphylaxis
blocks.text: Airway, breathing or circulation compromise with urticaria/angioedema → intramuscular adrenaline and emergency services (RCUK). Do not treat as “just hives”.

drugs.name: Cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine
drugs.dose: Licensed daily dose · Every day in CSU, not as needed

ladder.t: Remove triggers; avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, opioids if they aggravate; paracetamol preferred. Cool measures; avoid overheating and tight clothes.
Increase up to **4× licensed dose** (off-label); counsel sedation. Switch agent if one fails at high dose. Sedating antihistamine at night only if sleep is wrecked.
Short oral prednisolone (up to 7 days per CKS) **plus** antihistamine. Avoid repeated courses in CSU.
Dermatology / allergy for **omalizumab** (NICE TA), then other immunosuppressants. Montelukast sometimes on specialist advice; H2 blockers no longer routine.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **ACE-inhibitor angioedema**: Stop the ACEI, don’t rechallenge; antihistamines and steroids help poorly. ARB only with caution and advice.

refer.t: Lesions > 24 h with purpura: vasculitis work-up.
Fever, arthralgia, weight loss with urticarial rash: systemic disease / Schnitzler.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Anaphylaxis features.
Airway-threatening angioedema (ACEI or other).
Lesions lasting >24 h with purpura → vasculitis work-up.
Fever, arthralgia, weight loss with urticarial rash → systemic disease / Schnitzler consideration.
CSU uncontrolled on up-dosed antihistamine → refer.
**Anaphylaxis** (with respiratory or circulatory compromise).
Airway compromise from laryngeal or tongue angioedema.
Sleep loss, poor quality of life, anxiety and depression in chronic urticaria.
Acute urticaria usually settles within days to weeks.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria: about 50% remit within a year; some persist for more than 5 years.

pearls: “It isn’t an allergy to something you keep eating” — most CSU is internal.
Take the antihistamine every day, even on good days; step down slowly once controlled.
Patch testing investigates eczema, not wheals.
Always check BNF for residual renal/hepatic dosing and pregnancy.
Swelling without wheals on an ACE inhibitor: see [ACE-inhibitor angioedema](condition:ace-inhibitor-angioedema).
Wheals lasting more than 24 hours that bruise or burn: see [urticarial vasculitis](condition:urticarial-vasculitis).

quiz.q: How long does an individual urticarial wheal last?
quiz.a: Less than 24 hours, leaving normal skin. Longer with bruising suggests urticarial vasculitis.

quiz.q: First-line treatment for CSU and how to take it?
quiz.a: A second-generation H1 antihistamine (cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine) every day, not as needed.

quiz.q: Next step if uncontrolled after 2–4 weeks?
quiz.a: Up-dose to up to four times the licensed dose (off-label), then refer for omalizumab if still uncontrolled.

quiz.q: Lip swelling without wheals on ramipril?
quiz.a: ACE-inhibitor (bradykinin) angioedema: stop the ACEI; emergency care if the airway is threatened.

quiz.q: Is patch testing useful in urticaria?
quiz.a: No: it investigates delayed contact eczema, not wheals.
